prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of GLP-1 and the identification of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity.

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the one candidate on which all six opening ballots converge (five first places, one second). It offers an unbroken line from gut-hormone physiology and proglucagon processing, through identification of the biologically active peptide, to therapies that have changed the care of type 2 diabetes and obesity and now show cardiovascular and renal benefit, with emerging neurological interest. The discovery is clear, the mechanism is stable, efficacy has been confirmed in large independent outcome trials, and recognition is timely. I have moved my configuration from my opening ballot: I now credit Mojsov in place of Knudsen, so that the prize rests on the discoveries of physiology and of the active peptide rather than on industrial analogue design.
statement.case_against: The credit structure is the weak point. Four names are credited and only three can be named, and the priority claims around identification of the active GLP-1 peptide (Mojsov versus other groups not listed) cannot be settled from the supplied evidence. Dropping Knudsen leaves out the person who designed the long-acting analogues that actually reached patients, and a prize that honours the physiology but not the drug can be criticised as incomplete. A GLP-1 prize may also be seen as favouring a field with large commercial interest, although that should not weigh against the science.

responses.point: A basic-science-centred GLP-1 prize would more naturally name Drucker, Holst and Mojsov and omit the industrial developer Knudsen.
responses.response: I partly agree and have changed my configuration accordingly. In my opening ballot I named Knudsen, because the line from physiology to a drug is what makes the discovery exceptional. On reflection the discovery-level credit for the active peptide and its physiology is more defensible with Mojsov, and Knudsen's role is development work that other prizes and the clinical record already recognise. I would still want us to note the omission openly and not treat it as costless.

responses.point: The unfolded protein response (B032, Walter and Mori) should rank first: it is conceptually original, mechanistically complete, confirmed for three decades and arguably overdue.
responses.response: I agree that B032 is among the strongest basic-science cases and I ranked it second. We differ on what drives the choice. UPR is a conceptual advance whose human disease links (diabetes, neurodegeneration, cancer) are real but indirect, whereas GLP-1 combines a comparable mechanistic story with documented, very large effects on patients. Your point about Ron and Kaufman being outside the credit list is a genuine limit on B032's attribution, so I do not think its clean two-person pairing is as clean as it looks. I keep it as my first alternative and would support it if GLP-1 stalls on credit.

responses.point: B007 (BCL-2) should rank third, because it showed that BCL-2 controls cell survival rather than proliferation and led to venetoclax, but a four-name credit cannot fit.
responses.response: I accept the scientific significance of BCL-2 and the strength of its translational validation through venetoclax. The attribution problem you identify is, I think, more serious than a matter of fitting four names into three places. The Tsujimoto and Croce work on the translocation and the ced-9 link make the discovery chain hard to assign, and any three-person selection would leave out someone with a strong claim. I place it below cGAS-STING and CAR-T for this round, and I would reconsider it only if the committee can agree a defensible allocation.

responses.point: Anti-TNF therapy in rheumatoid arthritis (B006, Feldmann and Maini) deserves rank two as a very mature, clean two-person case that changed outcomes for millions of patients.
responses.response: The clinical impact is not in doubt. B006 is not on our shortlist, so I cannot argue for it as a configuration in this round. Within the shortlist, I would ask whether maturity is working fully in its favour: a discovery that has been in use for over two decades, with credit claims from others such as Vilcek, Cerami and Kollias that you list yourself, carries an attribution risk comparable to the CAR-T case. I would take your point as support for valuing autoimmunity and cytokine biology, which B013 also addresses mechanistically.

responses.point: Optogenetics (B046) is original, broadly enabling and has transformed circuit analysis, but six credited names force a difficult three-person choice.
responses.response: I agree that optogenetics is a major method, and as a neurologist I see its value for mechanism. My reservation is the one you state: there is no cleanly defensible subset of three among Miesenböck, Bamberg, Nagel, Hegemann, Boyden and Deisseroth, and the therapeutic payoff (retinal vision restoration) is still early. A prize for a tool whose human benefit is still ahead is a harder case than GLP-1, and I would not put it in the preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority in identifying the active GLP-1 peptide can be credited at the level of Drucker and Holst, given disputed historical accounts that the supplied text does not resolve.
Whether a prize that omits Knudsen, the designer of liraglutide and semaglutide, would be seen as incomplete for a discovery whose importance rests on therapy.
Whether a two-part configuration (for example GLP-1 alongside UPR or CAR-T) would be preferable to a single GLP-1 prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. I worked with Paul Greengard and have about twenty co-authored works with Thomas Perlmann, but neither is a credited name on any shortlisted ballot. I note the Perlmann co-authorship for transparency.
